templates.name: Addition/similarity: a further item of the same kind
Contrast: established view or appearance, then a finding that breaks it
Contrast: positive claim, then a limiting fact about the same subject
Cause/effect: condition, principle or evidence, then its consequence
Cause/effect: need or judgment, then the action it motivates
Concession: grant, then the main claim resumes (but / Still)
Concession: supported claim, then a fact that qualifies it
Emphasis: stronger same-direction fact (content-contrast trap at hard)
Purpose and aptness: goal then deliberate act, or a fitting echo
Specification/restatement: exact content or plain rewording
Sequence/time: next step, earlier or later event, end of a long effort
Culmination, alternative and place (ultimately, alternatively, there)
Example: general claim, then one named instance

items.passage: Chinese architect Wang Shu conceived the Ningbo History Museum as a building whose walls would preserve the remnants of villages demolished nearby. ______ some of those walls are reinforced concrete, molded against bamboo formwork. Still, across much of the facade, bricks and tiles salvaged from the razed dwellings, some a century old, are fitted together in wapan, a traditional patchwork masonry technique.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says the walls were meant to preserve the remains of demolished villages. The blank sentence grants a point that cuts against this aim: some walls are concrete, not salvaged material. The next sentence, beginning with “Still,” returns to the main claim: much of the facade is made of salvaged bricks and tiles. “Of course” is the transition that concedes a point before such a turn.

A.why_wrong: Concrete walls are not a more precise account of how the walls preserve village remains; the clause names an exception to that aim.

B.why_wrong: The concrete walls are not a second case like the museum’s aim of preserving village remains; they are an exception the writer concedes before turning back with “Still.”

D.why_wrong: The aim of preserving village remains does not cause some walls to be made of concrete.

sources.what: Ningbo Museum opened 2008; salvaged bricks and stone, wapan, concrete and bamboo walls, hundred-year-old materials
facade of bricks and tiles from the remains of farmers' homes; concrete walls on a wood-and-bamboo frame
bricks and roof tiles salvaged from demolition sites; continuity of the region's history

items.notes: Band-7 target, but spec/rw/band7/transitions.md finds no band-7 K1 official item (K1 tops out at band 6) and says not to push it. Written as the strongest band-6 K1: dense register; the blank sentence names the same walls as A and ends with salvaged materials, so Specifically and In fact pull on a first read; no phantom-sequence or summary decoy. No contrast decoy because rw_options excludes contrast next to a concession key. Register 5.48 chars/word.

fixes: safety solve: 'In fact,' was defensible in its corrective sense; replaced with a decoy of a plainly different relation, awaiting a fresh safety solve

band7.why: K1_grant_turn has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/transitions.md section 5), so it cannot be band 7; it stands as a strong band 6 on the f5959727 frame (Of course ... Still), register 5.48. "In fact" next to a concession key is a CB decoy (176edca6, Granted key).

items.passage: Around 100 CE, Claudia Severa, a Roman commander’s wife, sent her friend Sulpicia Lepidina a wooden tablet inviting her to a birthday celebration. Excavated at Vindolanda, near Hadrian’s Wall, the tablet is frequently identified as the earliest surviving Latin written in a woman’s own hand. ______ a professional scribe wrote out most of the invitation; Severa personally added only the final lines.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The text says the tablet is often called the earliest surviving Latin written by a woman. The last sentence limits that claim without overturning it: a scribe wrote most of the tablet, and only the final lines are in Severa’s own hand. “Granted” signals this kind of qualification.

B.why_wrong: A scribe writing most of the invitation is not an instance of the tablet being in Severa’s own hand; it qualifies that claim, since she wrote only the final lines.

C.why_wrong: Calling the tablet the earliest Latin by a woman does not cause a scribe to have written most of it.

D.why_wrong: The sentence is not one more point in favor of the claim; it qualifies the claim by showing that only part of the tablet is Severa’s writing.

sources.what: Tab. Vindol. 291: c. AD 97-105, Severa wife of Aelius Brocchus, main text in a scribe's hand, closing greeting in her own hand, earliest known Latin by a woman
British Museum, Vindolanda tablets

fixes: safety solve: 'In fact,' was defensible in its corrective sense; replaced with a decoy of a plainly different relation, awaiting a fresh safety solve

band7.why: band_target 6; mirrors 176edca6 (Granted key, In fact decoy, qualifying last sentence).

items.passage: Ornithologists long assumed that songbirds migrating from Europe to tropical Africa cross the Sahara in a single nonstop flight lasting about forty hours. Radar observations by Heiko Schmaljohann and colleagues in Mauritania undermined that assumption; ______ the team found, songbirds took off shortly after sunset from the open desert, evidently having spent the daylight hours resting on the ground rather than flying.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first clause of the second sentence says radar observations undermined the idea of a nonstop flight. The clause after the blank tells what the team found and how common it was: in many cases, songbirds took off at sunset after resting in the desert all day. “In many cases” introduces this more precise account of the finding.

A.why_wrong: Nothing in the clause concedes a point against the radar evidence; birds resting in the desert is exactly how the evidence undermined the nonstop account.

B.why_wrong: The radar observations did not cause the birds to take off at sunset; the takeoffs are what the observations recorded.

C.why_wrong: The clause is not a further, separate point; it spells out what the team found, which is the very evidence that undermined the assumption.

sources.what: long assumed 40 h non-stop flight; radar at three sites in Mauritania; departures right after sunset, birds spent the day in the plain desert; most songbirds cross intermittently
Schmaljohann thesis, radar at three Mauritanian sites 2003-2004

items.notes: Band-7 moves (spec/rw/band7/transitions.md section 5, S1 frequency form): the clause before the blank challenges a long-held account and B gives the common case; B's content (resting, not flying nonstop) reads as a contrast with the old view, so the concession decoy pulls; key outside the core 13. 'more often' is not in rw_options' inventory, so the frequency key is 'in many cases'. Decoys differ from d3b7d7a3's (that said / moreover replace nevertheless / additionally). Section 6: key not core 13; no sequence or summary decoy; surface-contrast proxy passes (adversative decoy, 'rather than' in the blank's clause); interrupter 'the team found,' added in review as in d3b7d7a3. Gate passes (register 5.38 chars/word after review).

fixes: passage: dropped "at three sites" to hold length
passage: added the interrupter "the team found," after the blank (band-7 S1 recipe, model d3b7d7a3); it ties the clause to the radar finding, so "moreover" cannot read as a further, separate fact
C why_wrong tied to "the team found"

band7.why: Matches d3b7d7a3: a long-held account undermined, then after a semicolon and the interrupter "the team found," the common case, keyed with a frequency connective outside the core 13 (bank exposure 1). "rather than flying" makes the clause look like a contrast, so "that said" pulls; "moreover" fails only because the clause is the finding itself. Section 6: key not core 13, no sequence or summary decoy, surface-contrast proxy passes, register 5.38.

items.passage: Stemborers, moths whose larvae tunnel into maize stalks, can devastate harvests throughout East Africa. Farmers have conventionally combated these pests with chemical insecticides. ______ they can practice push-pull, a strategy pioneered in Kenya: desmodium interplanted between the maize rows releases odors that repel the moths, while a perimeter of Napier grass attracts them away from the crop.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence names one way to protect maize from stemborers: chemical insecticides. The last sentence describes a different way to solve the same problem, planting desmodium and Napier grass. “Alternatively” signals this second option.

A.why_wrong: Push-pull is not an instance of using chemical insecticides; it is a different method.

C.why_wrong: Using insecticides does not lead to farmers practicing push-pull; the sentences describe two separate options.

D.why_wrong: The second sentence does not reword the first; it introduces a new method with new details.

sources.what: push-pull developed by icipe: desmodium volatiles repel stemborer moths, Napier grass attracts them
stemborers lay eggs in maize stems; farmers can lose much of a crop; pesticides are the usual response

fixes: explanation: "second sentence" twice; the second is the last sentence

band7.why: band_target 6; mirrors 9502ec65 (Alternatively key against example, cause and restatement decoys).

items.passage: Cuvier’s beaked whales routinely remain submerged far longer than their oxygen reserves would seemingly permit. Even so, the 222-minute dive documented in 2020 by researchers led by Nicola Quick was extraordinary for the species. ______ the median duration of the more than 3,600 foraging dives captured by the team’s satellite-linked transmitters was only 59 minutes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence claims that the 222-minute dive was extraordinary even for Cuvier’s beaked whales. The last sentence supports that claim: a typical dive lasted only about an hour, far less than 222 minutes. “Indeed” signals a fact that confirms and strengthens the previous claim.

A.why_wrong: The 59-minute median does not hold true in spite of the record dive; it is the evidence that the record dive was extraordinary.

C.why_wrong: The record dive did not cause the typical dive to be short; the median is evidence about the whales, not a result of the record.

D.why_wrong: The median is not a separate point added to the previous one; it is the support for the claim that the 222-minute dive was extraordinary.

sources.what: 222-minute dive, JEB 23 Sept 2020; 23 whales; median presumed foraging dive 59 min
Nicola Quick, Duke; 3,680 dives by 23 whales; seal-based calculations implied about half an hour

items.notes: Band-7 moves: content contrast with logical support (B's short typical dive looks like a reversal of the record, but it proves the record extraordinary); concession sentence ('Even so') in A primes a contrast reading; key outside the core 13; blank sentence-initial after a period, not the officials' semicolon frame, and no 'outlier'/'majority' wording. Section 6: key not core 13; no sequence or summary decoy; surface-contrast proxy passes ('only' in the blank sentence, adversative decoy); register 5.56 chars/word. Gate passes.

band7.why: Matches a266d876 and 47e238be: a record called extraordinary, then the typical case with the opposite value ("only 59 minutes"), keyed with indeed; "Even so" in sentence 2 primes a contrast reading, so "Nevertheless" pulls; decoys are CB's own set (false opposition, unearned cause, additive). Section 6: key not core 13, no sequence or summary decoy, surface-contrast proxy passes, register 5.52.

items.passage: Humans possess a single copy of TP53, a gene that instructs cells with damaged DNA either to repair the damage or to self-destruct before becoming cancerous. African elephants, ______ carry at least twenty copies, a redundancy that may explain why these enormous, long-lived animals so rarely succumb to cancer.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says humans have one copy of TP53. The second says elephants have at least twenty copies. “By contrast” marks the difference between the two species.

B.why_wrong: Elephants are not an example of humans having one copy; they have many more.

C.why_wrong: Elephants do not have a similar number of copies; twenty differs sharply from one.

D.why_wrong: The second sentence is about a different species with a different number of copies, not a rewording of the first.

sources.what: humans one TP53 copy, African elephants at least 20 copies; elephant cancer mortality 4.81% vs 11-25% in humans (Abegglen et al. 2015, JAMA)

items.passage: At his Bamako studio in the 1950s, Malian photographer Seydou Keïta encouraged sitters to pose with borrowed accessories, from wristwatches to a Vespa scooter, that conveyed cosmopolitan sophistication. ______ he hung boldly patterned textiles behind his subjects, replacing these backdrops every few years, a practice that now enables scholars to date individual portraits.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes one way Keïta shaped his portraits: lending sitters props. The second describes another: hanging patterned backdrops behind them. “Moreover” adds this second practice to the first.

A.why_wrong: The backdrops did not replace the props; Keïta used both.

B.why_wrong: Hanging backdrops is a new practice, not a rewording of lending props.

D.why_wrong: Lending props did not cause Keïta to hang patterned backdrops.

sources.what: studio props included watches, pens, radios, Western suits and a Vespa
lushly patterned backdrops and props now date periods of his career; Bamako studio in the 1950s and 1960s

items.passage: Lesley Nneka Arimah’s 2017 story collection What It Means When a Man Falls from the Sky frequently renders ordinary emotional experiences in fantastical terms. In “Who Will Greet You at Home,” prospective mothers must fashion infants from yarn or clay. ______ in the title story, mathematicians have devised calculations capable of removing a person’s grief.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says the collection often presents everyday emotions in fantastical terms. The next two sentences each describe a story that does this: one about longing for a child, one about grief. “Likewise” signals that the title story is a parallel case.

A.why_wrong: The title story does not hold true despite the first story; it works the same way.

B.why_wrong: The title story is a different story, not a rewording of the description of “Who Will Greet You at Home.”

C.why_wrong: One story’s premise does not cause the other story’s premise.

sources.what: Who Will Greet You at Home: women craft children from yarn, raffia or clay; first in The New Yorker 2015, collected 2017
title story: mathematicians allow humans to remove emotional pain from others

items.passage: In 2016, a University of Vermont team led by computational scientist Andrew Reagan charted the emotional trajectories of fiction on an unprecedented scale. ______ the researchers used sentiment-analysis software to score the happiness of the vocabulary in successive segments of 1,327 Project Gutenberg stories, tracing how each narrative’s mood rose and fell.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence states in general terms what the team did: it charted the emotional trajectories of fiction. The second sentence gives the exact procedure they used. “Specifically” introduces this more precise account.

A.why_wrong: The procedure does not contrast with the charting described before; it is how the charting was done.

C.why_wrong: Rating the words is not a separate project added to charting trajectories; it is how the trajectories were charted.

D.why_wrong: The second sentence does not describe a similar, separate case; it describes the same study in more detail.

sources.what: Reagan, Mitchell, Kiley, Danforth, Dodds 2016, EPJ Data Science: 1,327 Project Gutenberg stories, six core emotional arcs

items.passage: Among amphibians, lunglessness was known only in a large family of salamanders and in one caecilian; every frog examined had possessed lungs. On a 2007 expedition to Indonesian Borneo, ______ biologist David Bickford confirmed that Barbourula kalimantanensis, a flattened stream-dwelling frog, has no lungs, absorbing oxygen entirely through its skin.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says that every frog examined had lungs. The second reports a frog with no lungs at all, which breaks that pattern. “However” marks this contrast between the earlier record and the new finding.

A.why_wrong: The second sentence does not reword the claim that every frog examined had lungs; it reports a frog that breaks that pattern.

B.why_wrong: The earlier record of frogs with lungs did not cause Bickford’s finding of a lungless frog.

D.why_wrong: The lungless frog is not a particular case of frogs having lungs; it is an exception to that pattern.

sources.what: Barbourula kalimantanensis, first known lungless frog; Bickford, Iskandar, Barlian 2008, Current Biology; 2007 expedition; lunglessness probably evolved only three times

items.passage: In the late 1990s, a national electrification program connected thousands of rural households in South Africa’s KwaZulu-Natal province, where women had long spent many hours gathering firewood. Economist Taryn Dinkelman found that newly connected communities shifted sharply from wood to electricity for cooking. ______ women there became markedly more likely to hold paid jobs within five years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The text explains that women in the province had spent many hours gathering firewood and that electrified communities stopped cooking with wood. Freed from that work, women took paid jobs. “Hence” signals that this rise in employment is a consequence of the change described before it.

B.why_wrong: The rise in women’s employment did not happen in spite of the switch from wood; it followed from it.

C.why_wrong: Women taking paid jobs is not a similar case of switching fuels; it is a result of the switch.

D.why_wrong: Women holding paid jobs is a new fact, not a rewording of the shift from wood to electricity.

sources.what: Dinkelman, rural electrification roll-out in KwaZulu-Natal 1996-2001; shift away from wood; female employment rises within five years; women spend much time on fuel-wood collection

items.passage: In 2004, Cuban American painter Carmen Herrera, then 89, sold a canvas for the first time. Within a few years, her crisp, hard-edged geometric abstractions were attracting international acclaim. ______ she had labored for roughly six decades in near obscurity, exhibiting infrequently and receiving scant attention from dealers or critics.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first two sentences describe Herrera’s success beginning in 2004. The last describes the long period before that, when she worked in obscurity. “Previously” signals that the last sentence describes an earlier time.

A.why_wrong: Decades of obscurity are not similar to the acclaim described in the second sentence.

B.why_wrong: Her late success did not cause the obscurity, which came first.

C.why_wrong: Working in obscurity is not an example of selling paintings and drawing acclaim.

items.passage: Tsuda Umeko studied biology at Bryn Mawr College in Pennsylvania from 1889 to 1892. She returned to Japan convinced that Japanese women deserved an education as rigorous as the instruction available to men at the nation’s elite universities. ______ in 1900 she established the Women’s Institute of English Studies in Tokyo, holding its students to exacting academic standards.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence states Tsuda’s conviction that Japanese women deserved a rigorous education. The last describes the step she took to act on that belief: founding a demanding school for women. “With this in mind” signals an action taken to serve the goal just stated.

A.why_wrong: Founding the school did not happen regardless of her conviction; it followed from it.

C.why_wrong: Founding the school is not a similar, separate case; it is what she did because of her conviction.

D.why_wrong: The last sentence adds a new action and date; it does not reword her conviction.

items.passage: In Rwanda, the company Zipline uses drones to deliver blood supplies to rural hospitals. First, a health worker requests the necessary blood by text message. ______ employees at a Zipline distribution center package the order in a cardboard container and launch a drone by catapult. Finally, the drone releases the package, which descends by parachute.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The text lists the steps of a delivery in order, marked by “First” and “Finally.” Packing the box and launching the drone come after the order is placed and before the box is dropped. “Next” signals this middle step.

B.why_wrong: Packing and launching the drone is not an example of ordering blood; it is the following step.

C.why_wrong: Packing the order does not contrast with placing it; it continues the process.

D.why_wrong: The staff’s actions are not similar to the health worker’s; they are the next step.

items.passage: While incarcerated with other Japanese Americans in camps in California and Utah from 1942 to 1944, artist Miné Okubo produced hundreds of drawings documenting the cramped barracks and relentless dust storms of camp life. ______ in 1946, she published Citizen 13660, an illustrated memoir recounting her experiences through captioned drawings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes drawings Okubo made from 1942 to 1944. The second describes a book she published in 1946, after that period. “Later” signals that the second event came after the first.

A.why_wrong: Publishing the book did not happen in spite of the drawings; it grew out of them.

B.why_wrong: Publishing a book in 1946 is not similar to making drawings in the camps; it is a later event.

D.why_wrong: The book is not an example of the drawings she made in the camps.

items.passage: Portuguese merchants and missionaries, the first Europeans to reach Japan, arrived in the 1540s and remained influential there for nearly a century. Their language left enduring traces on Japanese vocabulary. ______ the Japanese word for bread, pan, derives from the Portuguese pão, and karuta, meaning “playing cards,” derives from the Portuguese carta.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence makes a general claim: Portuguese left traces on Japanese vocabulary. The last gives specific words that show this. “For example” introduces these instances.

A.why_wrong: The borrowed words do not exist in spite of the Portuguese influence; they are evidence of it.

B.why_wrong: The sentence does not describe something happening at the same time as the traders’ arrival; it gives instances of the claim.

C.why_wrong: Naming particular words adds specific instances; it does not reword the general claim.

items.notes: Loanwords pan and karuta and the 1540s arrival are standard facts; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: Beginning in 1979, Mexican photographer Graciela Iturbide spent years documenting everyday life in Juchitán, an Oaxacan town where Zapotec women dominate the bustling marketplaces and command considerable respect. ______ her photograph Nuestra Señora de las Iguanas depicts a Juchitán vendor gazing into the distance with live iguanas arranged like a crown on her head.

items.explanation: The first sentence says Iturbide spent years photographing daily life and women in Juchitán. The second describes one photograph from that work. “For instance” introduces this example.

C.why_wrong: The photograph is not a result of the information about Juchitán’s markets; it is an instance of Iturbide’s documentation.

items.passage: The frigid waters of the Southern Ocean contain abundant dissolved oxygen. This may explain how Antarctic icefish survive without hemoglobin, the protein that transports oxygen in the bloodstream of other vertebrates and gives blood its characteristic red color. ______ the blood of icefish is nearly transparent, and their gills are creamy white.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence says icefish lack hemoglobin, the protein that makes blood red. Without it, their blood is nearly clear and their gills are pale. “As a result” signals this consequence.

A.why_wrong: Clear blood does not contrast with lacking hemoglobin; it follows from it.

B.why_wrong: Clear blood is not a similar fact about another case; it is the result of the missing hemoglobin.

D.why_wrong: Clear blood is not an example of the ocean holding oxygen; it is a consequence of lacking hemoglobin.

items.notes: Icefish lacking hemoglobin is a standard biology fact; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: In Australia, where participation in federal elections was voluntary, fewer than 60 percent of eligible citizens voted in 1922. Two years later, parliament passed legislation requiring all eligible citizens to vote and penalizing those who failed to do so without a legitimate excuse. ______ turnout in the 1925 federal election exceeded 90 percent.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence describes a 1924 law that made voting compulsory and fined nonvoters. The last sentence reports that turnout then rose above 90 percent. “Consequently” signals that this rise resulted from the law.

B.why_wrong: The 1925 election came after the 1924 law, not before it.

C.why_wrong: High turnout did not happen in spite of the law; the law produced it.

D.why_wrong: The 1925 turnout is not an example of the law; it is the law’s result.

items.passage: Nigerian teacher Mohammed Bah Abba promoted a pot-in-pot cooler: one clay pot nested inside a larger one, with wet sand between them. B.why_wrong: The limitation is not similar to the benefit described before; it restricts it.

items.passage: When armed militants occupied Timbuktu, Mali, in 2012, librarian Abdel Kader Haidara feared that the city’s hundreds of thousands of centuries-old manuscripts, covering subjects from astronomy to law, would be destroyed. ______ he organized a secret operation in which couriers smuggled the manuscripts, packed in metal footlockers, hundreds of miles south to the capital, Bamako.
